extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), and applicants involved in double patenting and terminal disclaimer issues
extracted.subtask_short: double patenting examination and terminal disclaimers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, rejecting, and resolving double patenting issues in U.S. patent prosecution, including when and how to require or accept terminal disclaimers, how common ownership and joint research agreements affect prior art and double patenting analyses, and examiner form-paragraph practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance requirement for Section 121 protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 121 shields claims against a double patenting challenge only if 'consonance' exists between the divided groups of claims—that is, the line of demarcation between the independent and distinct inventions in the restriction requirement must be maintained. If that line is crossed, Section 121 protection does not apply. Even if consonance is lost, double patenting does not automatically follow if the requirements of Section 121 are met or if the claims are patentably distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations and case citations (Geneva Pharmaceuticals v. GlaxoSmithKline; Symbol Techs. v. Opticon; Gerber Garment Technology) illustrate that consonance depends on maintenance of the original division and that Section 121 aims to accommodate administrative convenience while protecting patentees from technical flaws in examination practice. If consonance is lost, examiners must still consider whether Section 121 requirements otherwise are satisfied or whether patentable distinctness exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer required despite common issue date
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on a common issue date alone cannot substitute for filing a terminal disclaimer to overcome a proper nonstatutory double patenting rejection. A common issue date does not avoid potential problems of dual ownership or ensure coextensive enforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants are cautioned that the Office cannot ensure common issue dates will occur; therefore, terminal disclaimers should be filed when necessary to overcome nonstatutory double patenting rejections rather than relying on expected common issue dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaiming multiple double patenting references (single vs multiple disclaimers)
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple conflicting patents/applications are cited in nonstatutory double patenting rejections in a single application, it is necessary before issuance to disclaim the terminal part of any patent term that would extend beyond the expiration date of each conflicting patent/application. A terminal disclaimer fee is required for each terminal disclaimer filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid multiple fees and ensure proper public notice, a single terminal disclaimer based on common ownership (or on a joint research agreement) may be filed where the term disclaimed is based on all conflicting, commonly owned nonstatutory double patenting references. However, each conflicting, commonly owned reference must be included in the disclaimer to avoid problems if common ownership later ceases. See 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3) which requires that the disclaimer include a provision limiting enforcement to the period of common ownership (and 1.321(d) for joint research agreements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements of a terminal disclaimer (per 37 CFR 1.321)
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer is a statement filed by an owner (in whole or in part) of a patent or patent to be granted used to disclaim or dedicate a portion of the entire term of all claims of a patent. The formal requirements are set forth in 37 CFR 1.321.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample terminal disclaimer forms and further filing/treatment guidance are provided in MPEP § 1490. Examiners and applicants should follow 37 CFR 1.321's content and procedural requirements (including required provisions limiting enforceability to the period of common ownership or per joint research agreement when applicable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimers required for continuing applications filed on/after June 8, 1995
rubrics_metrics.description: For utility/plant continuing applications filed on or after June 8, 1995, patents issue with a 20-year term from the appropriate earliest filing date per amended 35 U.S.C. 154(a)(2), but a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321 is still required to overcome a nonstatutory double patenting rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two reasons support requiring terminal disclaimers despite the 20-year rule: (1) patent term adjustments under 35 U.S.C. 154(b) may alter expiration dates unless a terminal disclaimer fixes expiration, and (2) 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3) requires enforceability limitations tied to common ownership to prevent harassment by multiple parties. Examiners should cite this MPEP section when applicants argue terminal disclaimers are unnecessary based on filing-date term calculations. See cited Federal Register/O.G. notices and cases (e.g., AbbVie v. Kennedy Institute).

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of a terminal disclaimer before issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a terminal disclaimer is filed in an application and the claims are later canceled or shown to be patentably distinct from the reference claims, the terminal disclaimer may be withdrawn before patent issuance by filing a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 requesting withdrawal of the recorded terminal disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A terminal disclaimer may not be withdrawn after patent issuance. See MPEP § 1490, subsection VIII, for full withdrawal procedure and considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and threshold for common ownership (35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) and pre-AIA 103(c)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications or patents are 'commonly owned' under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) if they were wholly owned by the same person(s) or organization(s) not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention; under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1) common ownership is determined at the time the claimed invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common ownership requires 100% ownership of the subject matter that would otherwise be prior art and 100% ownership of the claimed invention. Partial ownership (<100%) does not establish common ownership for these exceptions. See MPEP § 717.02(a) and MPEP § 2146.02 for detailed definitions and evaluation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint research agreement criteria for treating references as commonly owned (35 U.S.C. 102(c) and pre-AIA 103(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter disclosure and a claimed invention can be treated as commonly owned under the joint research agreement provisions if the disclosure was developed and the invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the relevant date, the claimed invention resulted from activities within the scope of that agreement, and the application discloses (or is amended to disclose) the names of the parties to the agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CREATE Act (pre-AIA 103(c)) and 35 U.S.C. 102(c) have similar requirements but differ in timing: 102(c) is keyed to effective filing date; CREATE Act focuses on the date the invention was made and applies only to obviousness (not anticipation or double patenting). Definitions: 'joint research agreement' = written contract/grant/cooperative agreement among two or more persons for experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. See MPEP §§ 2146 and 717 for more details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting rejections and how to overcome them
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonstatutory double patenting rejections can be overcome by disclaiming the terminal portion of the term of the later patent under 37 CFR 1.321(c) (for common ownership) or 1.321(d) (for joint research agreement situations), and including the requisite enforceability-limiting provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclaimer must include the enforcement limitation tied to common ownership or joint research agreement as appropriate. Even where prior art exceptions/disqualifications apply, examiners must consider whether double patenting rejections are appropriate and whether the terminal disclaimer remedy is applicable. Guidance cross-references MPEP §§ 717.02, 2146.02, and 1490.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to make both double patenting and prior art rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the facts support both bases, the examiner should make both a double patenting rejection based on common ownership and an appropriate prior art rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 and/or 103. Until an applicant properly invokes a joint research agreement exception or prior-art disqualification, the examiner should NOT apply a double patenting rejection based on a joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must ensure proper sequencing: make both rejections when warranted; but do not apply joint-research-based double patenting rejections until the applicant has established the exception/disqualification conditions. See MPEP §§ 706.07(a), 717.02(c), and 804, subsection VI for timing and finality considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and finality of double patenting rejections (office action practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on when an Office action that includes a new subsequent double patenting rejection based upon a reference subject to a joint research agreement may be made final, and related timing issues for issuing rejections and form paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference MPEP §§ 706.07(a), 717.02(c), and 804 subsection VI. Examiners should follow procedural guidelines to avoid premature final rejections where applicant has not had opportunity to demonstrate statutory exceptions or to submit terminal disclaimers. The MPEP charts summarize permissible combinations of rejections and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining invention priority (when required and when not)
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination of priority is not required when two inventions are commonly owned as set forth in 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where common ownership applies, the earlier invention cannot be used as prior art against the later, so priority determinations are unnecessary. However, when the provisions do not apply, examiners may require identification of the prior inventor under 37 CFR 1.78(g) or other rules; failure to comply with such a requirement may result in abandonment unless conflicting claims are eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.78(g) requirements for identifying ownership/prior inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application (or patent under reexamination) and at least one other application naming different inventors are owned by the same party and contain patentably indistinct claims, and there is no record statement indicating common ownership on the relevant date, the Office may require the applicant/assignee to state whether the claimed inventions were commonly owned or to indicate which named inventor is the prior inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs (e.g., 8.27.aia, 8.27.fti, 8.28.aia, etc.) may be used to require this information. The assignee must comply to avoid abandonment unless conflicting claims are eliminated. If the assignee asserts common ownership under the relevant statute, no further priority determination is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs and examiner notes in double patenting situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should use specified form paragraphs (e.g., 8.27.aia, 8.27.fti, 8.28.aia, 8.28.fti, 8.28.01.aia, etc.) tailored to whether the case is examined under AIA (first-inventor-to-file) or pre-AIA (first-to-invent) provisions, whether inventions are the same or merely not patentably distinct, and whether common ownership has been established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph guidance includes which brackets to fill (e.g., insert patent/application numbers), when to include companion paragraphs (e.g., 8.28.01.aia must follow 8.28.aia), when to add prior-art form paragraphs, and examiner cautions (e.g., do not use 'same invention' paragraph if one invention would have been obvious over the other; use the 'not patentably distinct' paragraph instead). Also note instructions to include provisional/statutory double patenting rejections via form paragraphs 8.31/8.32 where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine preventing multiple patents to the same invention (double patenting principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected for double patenting to prevent an organization from obtaining two or more patents with different expiration dates covering nearly identical subject matter; claims must be patentably distinct, not merely different in form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited precedent (In re Zickendraht; In re Christensen) supports that more than mere formal differences are required for entitlement to a second patent. Examiners should apply nonstatutory double patenting doctrine when claims lack patentable distinctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and scope of the CREATE Act (treatment of non-commonly owned joint research agreement references)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CREATE Act (Public Law 108-453) permits an applicant or patentee who is party to a joint research agreement to disqualify certain prior art that is otherwise available only under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f),(g) for purposes of obviousness, thereby allowing non-commonly owned patents/applications subject to a qualifying joint research agreement to be treated as commonly owned for obviousness determinations under pre-AIA 103(c)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To invoke CREATE, conditions must be met: (A) later invention not anticipated by earlier; (B) claimed invention made by/on behalf of parties to the joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (C) invention resulted from activities within the scope of the agreement; (D) the patent application discloses/amends to disclose names of the parties. CREATE applies only to obviousness (not to anticipation or double patenting) and focuses on the date the invention was made (unlike 35 U.S.C. 102(c)). See MPEP § 2146.02 for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of prior art exceptions/disqualifications in double patenting analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art exception in 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) and the prior-art disqualification in pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) are not determinative of whether there is a common applicant/owner for double patenting analysis; the statutory 'same person' requirement strictly requires identical owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must determine ownership at the appropriate time (effective filing date for 102(b)(2)(C), time of invention for pre-AIA 103(c)) and not conflate invocation of these exceptions with the separate analysis of common ownership needed for double patenting. The guidance in this section pertains to double patenting analyses only when the subject matter in the reference is excepted or disqualified as prior art under the cited provisions; cross-reference MPEP §§ 717.02 et seq., 2146.02, and 804 subsection VI.
